title: The Truth About Who You've Become
passages:
First light came up gray and held. Rusk’s barge slid alongside the Marrow with no running lights, no engine note, just the wet slap of fenders against salvaged hull and the creak of the Marrow’s mooring lines taking the weight. He stepped over the rail like he owned the rung, coat heavy with salt, one hand in his pocket working Teo’s spare medicine cartridges like a rosary.

Sol stood at the wheelhouse door, hands flat on the frame. “You’re early, Rusk. The storm hasn’t turned yet.”

“First light is the turn,” Rusk said. He smiled, and it didn’t reach his eyes. “The Factor wants the cold-case’s value. Twelve thousand. Or the Marrow itself. You got neither on the manifest, so I’m taking the boat.”

“You’re taking nothing,” Sol said. “We surfaced with nothing. Ask Nia.”

Nia didn’t look up from the chart table, pencil scratching the log. “Twelve thousand’s a lie. The case was sealed. Nobody opened it.”

Rusk pulled one cartridge from his coat and held it up to the light. Clear plastic, amber liquid inside, Teo’s name scratched on the label in Nia’s hand. “I got three of these as earnest. The kid needs one every twelve hours. He’s down to his last.” He let it disappear back into his coat. “Hand over the case value, sign the boat over to the Factor, or I start counting cartridges instead of hours.”

Dey coughed from the deck mat, wet and ragged, each breath longer than the last. Nia’s pencil stopped.

Sol’s voice stayed level. “The boat’s not for sale. The kids aren’t either. You want the cold case, go dive it yourself. Forty-two meters. See how long you last.”

Rusk’s hand stayed in his pocket. “I don’t dive. I collect. And I collect at first light. You got until the storm turns to change your mind.” He nodded past her, toward the hatch where Wren stood. “Tell your reader I’ll be back. With lights.”

He turned and stepped over the rail, the barge already drifting off into the flat water. Sol didn’t move until the barge had drifted clear and was nothing but a shadow in the rain.

Then Wren said, “He knows my name, Sol.”

Sol turned. “What?”

“The barge channel. Last night. He called me by name before he cut off.”

Sol touched the cut seal crimp in her pocket, the metal edges biting her palm. “Then he’s got more than the cartridges.”

A voice crackled from the deck speaker, thin and distant: *Wren.* Not Rusk. Not the barge. The line was dead, the speaker unpowered, and the voice came anyway, wet as saltwater in the lungs.

The speaker clicked once and went dead. Wren stared at it a beat longer, then caught Sol by the sleeve.

"Come with me. Now, before he's back with his lights."

Sol didn't pull away, which told Wren something. "The reader?"

"The reader."

The pod was a coffin of a room behind the wheelhouse, barely wide enough for the chair and the deck reader bolted to the bench — a scabbed gray box that took a diver's slate, the recorder strapped to every diver's chest, and rebuilt the hours their minds had dropped, stitching depth and heart rate and the slate's own clock into something you could stand and watch. Wren had built the thing. She'd also built a whole career on deciding which of those hours a person got to keep.

She dropped into the chair and slotted Sol's slate. Her hands were steady. That was the worst of it, how steady.

"Sol. I cut an hour out of you last night. I'm giving it back."

Sol's face hardly moved. "Why now?"

"Because Rusk knows my name and the deep keeps saying it too, and I'm done being the only one who remembers things." Wren thumbed play. "Watch."

The reader threw gray light on the bulkhead, and there was the deck, last night, the drum screaming, the cold-case swinging in its cradle with the Factor's drone lights crawling over the water. There was Sol at the rail. A broker's voice came off the slate, thin through the storm. *Twelve thousand, Captain. Set it down and step back.*

Wren had watched this hour a dozen times before she cut it. She still wasn't ready.

On the wall, Sol's hand came up — not to the case, to the cradle release, where Nia and Teo had been sealed in the cold-box on the last of the hospital air. The Sol on the wall looked at the drone, said something the storm ate, and brought the release down. The drone went into the sea in a sheet of sparks and the drum took them all up on its last pull.

In the pod, the real Sol watched herself do it. Her jaw worked once.

"That's your twelve thousand," Wren said.

"I know what it was." Sol's voice had gone rough. "I don't remember deciding."

"Nobody does. That's what the depth takes." Wren reached for the slate. "There's eleven seconds more. Those are mine, not yours. I cut them out of my own log and I can't tell you why, so don't ask."

She played it.

The pod filled with her own voice, close and cracked with cold, coming from somewhere forty-two meters down and a night she couldn't account for: *I swear it. I'll bring the winch. Three times if that's what it takes. I'll bring the winch.*

Then nothing. The light snapped off.

Sol looked at her. "You said that last night. Right before you went over the side."

"I've never been down there in my life." Wren's hands had finally started to shake. "I've got fifty-two minutes gone off my own deck log, a dead channel saying my name, and a knot I tied that I don't remember tying. Something down there knows what I did. It might be me."

Sol reached over and stopped the slate with two fingers, the way you'd still a swinging compass.

"Then we don't guess," she said. "But first — you're standing next to me when he comes back. Both eyes open this time."

Out on the flat water, faint and closing, an engine turned over.

The engine note grew, a slow chug that vibrated through the Marrow's ribs. Wren left the reader running, slate still slotted, and followed Sol up the ladder to the deck. Rain needled her face, cold and clean after the pod's recycled air.

Rusk's barge was close enough now to see the pitted plate of its bow, the winch drum lashed amidships with chain instead of cable. No running lights. No name painted on the hull. Just a factor's mark burned into the port gunwale, old salt eating the edges.

Rusk stood at his rail, one boot on the fender, coat collar turned up against the wind. He held a thermos in his gloved hand, steam curling from the lid. He didn't put it down when they reached the Marrow's rail.

"Captain," he called. "Reader. First light's past. The storm's turning. My patience turned with it."

Sol didn't glance at Wren. She planted her feet on the wet deck, weight forward, the cut seal crimp still biting her palm. "We don't have twelve thousand. You know we don't."

"Then the boat," Rusk said. He sipped from the thermos, slow and deliberate. "The Factor's generous. He'll take the hull and call the debt square. Your crew can swim for high ground."

"The boat's not for sale," Sol said. Her voice carried flat across the water. "The kids aren't either."

Rusk's eyes flicked to the chart table hatch where Nia sat, pencil poised. To the deck mat where Dey's breathing hitched ragged and wet. Back to Sol. "Sentiment's expensive, Captain. You chose the children over the case last night. The Factor saw the drone feed. He knows the value walked off in a cold-box." He set the thermos on the rail. "So what's the play? You got a vault in the bilge I missed?"

Sol reached into her coat and pulled out a key on a lanyard. Not the wheelhouse key. Not the drum locker. A small brass key, salt-dulled, on a loop of orange twine. She tossed it to Wren.

"Forward hold. Port side. Two crates, Factor's seal wire intact."

Wren caught it. The metal was cold through her gloves. "Sol —"

"Go," Sol said. "Both crates. Bring them to the rail."

Wren didn't argue. She moved fast, ladder down, hatch dogged, corridor forward past the bunkroom where Salas slept on the impact-wrench bottle, past the head where the cold-box hummed its steady complaint. The forward hold smelled of diesel and old rope. Two white crates sat lashed to the deck ring, each stamped with the Mercy General cross and the Factor's red seal wire, unbroken.

She unlashed the first. Heavy. Dense. The second the same. She dragged them aft, one at a time, legs burning, the Marrow rolling under her. Sol waited at the rail, unmoving. Rusk watched from the barge, thermos forgotten.

Wren heaved the first crate over the Marrow's rail. It landed on the fender with a solid thump. The second followed. She braced her hands on the wet wood, breathing hard.

"Pharmacy pocket," Sol said to Rusk. "Forty-two meters. Sealed cases, full course antivirals, broad-spectrum antibiotics, pain management — enough to stock a clinic for a season. Twelve thousand's lowball. You know it."

Rusk didn't move for a long moment. The rain fell straight down now, no wind, the calm before the turn. He looked at the crates on his fender, then at Sol, then at Wren braced against the rail with salt in her eyelashes.

"Pharmacy pocket," he said. "Forty-two meters. You're telling me you dove Mercy General's sealed pocket, brought up two Factor crates, and you're handing them over instead of the hull."

"Dove it," Sol said. "Lost a diver doing it. Nearly lost another bringing the winch. The crates are intact. Seal wire unbroken. You can count them yourself or take my word. Your call."

Rusk's jaw tightened. He stepped onto the Marrow's rail, boots finding purchase on the wet gunwale, and dropped to the deck without using the ladder. Close up he smelled of diesel and something sharper — ozone, maybe, or the cold iron of the deep. He went to the first crate, crouched, and ran a gloved finger over the red seal wire. Intact. He produced a multi-tool from his coat, snipped the wire, and cracked the lid.

White vials in foam cutouts. Rows of them, each labeled in the Factor's cramped script. Rusk didn't count aloud. His eyes moved fast, throat working. He snapped the lid shut, moved to the second crate, repeated the motion. Snip. Crack. Scan. Snap.

"Broad-spectrum," he muttered. "Antivirals. Pain management. Full courses." He stood, wiping his gloves on his coat. "Twelve thousand was the cold-case bounty. This is thirty, maybe forty on the highland market. You're giving me the profit margin."

"The debt was twelve," Sol said. "The rest is what it cost us. You want to argue value with the Factor, take it up with him. These crates clear the Marrow, clear the children, clear the berths we need before the storm turns. That's the deal."

Rusk was quiet. He looked at the crates, then at the Marrow's patched hull, the jury-rigged winch, the deck mat where Dey's breathing hitched ragged beneath Nia's pencil. His hand went to his coat pocket — the pocket holding Teo's cartridges.

"You're a hard woman, Captain," he said. "Harder than the Factor gave you credit for."

"Factor doesn't give credit. He collects."

"Yeah." Rusk reached in, pulled out three clear cartridges, amber liquid catching the gray light. Teo's name in Nia's hand. He held them out across the rail, arm extended, not looking at Sol. "Earnest's returned. The boy keeps his course."

Sol took them. Her fingers brushed his glove — cold, wet, callused. She didn't flinch. "He's not a bargaining chip."

"Wasn't treating him like one." Rusk turned back to his barge, grabbed the rail, hauled himself up in one motion. He didn't look at Wren. "Reader. You got a name on the deep end. Might want to ask yourself why."

The barge's engine coughed to life, a low chug that shook the water. Rusk cast off his lines with practiced motions, the Marrow rocking in the wake. He stood at his wheel, one hand on the throttle, the crates lashed behind him. The Factor's mark on the gunwale caught the light as he turned the bow east, toward the high ground and the arcology's waiting docks.

"Storm's turning," he called back, voice carrying over the water. "You got berths to buy. Don't waste the daylight."

The barge pulled away, gathering speed, the wake spreading wide. Sol stood at the rail until it was a dark smudge on the horizon, three cartridges warm in her palm.

The bunkroom smelled of wet steel and the sweet chemical tang of the impact-wrench bottle, the little cylinder bled off a pneumatic tool that Salas had been sucking on since the drum brought him up. It was down to a whisper. Whatever it had left was his.

He woke the way divers wake, all at once, hand going to the valve at his teeth before his eyes were open. Then he looked at Wren kneeling by the bunk, and she watched him not know her. It crossed his face like weather.

"You're not my medic," he said.

"No."

"Then get off my air."

"It's your air." Wren kept her hands where he could see them. "Bottle's got twenty minutes in it. You want to spend them arguing, that's a diver's right."

Nia stood in the hatch with the three cartridges in her fist, rolling them like dice. "He wakes up rude. That's a good sign. Teo's the same."

"Who's Teo." Not a question. There was no lift in it at all.

Wren's stomach went down and kept going. "The boy you went back for."

Salas's eyes went to the ceiling, hunting. His hand found the orange twine still knotted round his wrist and turned it over like he was checking a splice. "There was a boy. I sealed him and his sister in the cold-case, put them in the float cradle, sent them up. That floats. Everybody knows that floats. Then I went back down for the boy's medicine, because he was on his last course and the case had a whole shelf." He stopped. "I went down at slack. It was still slack when I got there."

"It's been fourteen months," Wren said.

"Not possible."

"It's the depth. It takes what's under it, and you were under it a long time."

"Then it can hand it back." He said it flat, and he believed it, and that was worse than shouting.

Sol's boots stayed out in the corridor, giving the old man the room.

"Salas." Wren leaned in. "You called somebody, over and over. *Tell the kid to keep going.* Which kid?"

His face didn't change, but something behind it went looking. "The one on the mat," he said, meaning Dey. Then his mouth kept moving without him. "Bayo."

Nia's dice stopped.

"Who's Bayo?" Wren said.

Salas stared at his own hand. "I don't know. I said it. I don't know whose it is." He laughed once, an ugly sound. "That's a new one. Losing a name while it's still in my mouth."

Then he saw the slate strapped to his chest, the recorder every diver wears, tally light steady. He thumbed the log open with a diver's shortcut scroll, and Wren heard her own night come out of it in his voice, thin and patient. *Wren. Wren. Bring the winch.* A year of it stacked in rows, each one stamped with a depth and a time, every call one he couldn't remember making.

"Turn it off," he said.

"It's not on. It's a record."

"Same thing." He found the erase bar with his thumb. "A record's a hook. Somebody reads it, somebody comes down. Nobody comes down for me. I already got a kid left too long in the cold because I went back for a bottle, and I can't even remember doing it."

He pressed.

The slate chimed. The wheelhouse chimed back through the bulkhead, twice. Dey's slate chirped out on the deck mat where he lay breathing wet. Down in the pod the deck reader woke its lamp and started copying.

Nia looked at the chart table, at the paper log in its clip under her pencil, then at Salas, and her mouth did something that wasn't a smile.

"It's on mine," she said. "That's six."

"Six what."

"Six copies. Paper doesn't take an erase, old man." She tapped the pencil against the clip. "Congratulations. You're on the record. So's the kid. Whichever one you meant."

The bottle hissed down another notch. Salas's thumb stayed on the erase bar, and he looked past Wren through the open hatch, at the flat gray light coming down, like something out there had just heard its name read out loud.
